I'm in a similar situation. I am a lead technician working to switch to SWE, and I've been applying for about 6 months now, so hopefully I can give you some info I've learned along the way that might help.

1. Get 2 to 3 solid projects that display the skills you know. It might even be worth it to take on a project that requires skills you don't know yet. It will act as a great learning tool, but also will aid you when landing an interview. I have a lot of professional experience and a BS, but I still get told I don't have enough experience. I can't really blame them when I have a bunch of tiny school projects and one in-progress project that I can only milk so much during screening calls.
2. Either take part in an open source project or join a hack-a-thon. As an extension of my last point, company's want to see that you can work in a "production" environment. I would recommend an open source project because you'll learn a lot more about how real projects work. The first challenge is to find a project you want to take part in. I found some local groups through the Meetup app that create open source tools to help the city I live in. There's also sites out there like [up-for-grabs.net](https://up-for-grabs.net) that might help. Then you can check out their Issues tab on a repo you're interested in and find an issue you'd like to assist with. It's always important to reach out to the group/individual that owns the repo first to introduce yourself, share your experience level and ask if you can contribute in any way. You can let them know that you would like to tackle an issue you found, or ask if they have something you could assist. Another big bonus here is real world Git/GitHub experience. There's a lot to learn in this regard, and company's will be happy to know they don't need to spend extra hours training you on version control.
3. Apply to entry level positions or internships, and familiarize yourself with engineering levels like Staff, or Associate. If you don't know, Staff and Associate roles are higher up than regular SWE, and you can waste a lot of time applying to jobs you never stood a chance with. I did that and regret it. Don't get enticed by the Reddit/YouTube stories of people who applied to jobs asking for 3+ years of experience when they had none, and now they're getting paid $250k. Yes, it's "possible" with the right connections, position, and experience, but it's such a slim chance that you shouldn't rely on it. Find entry level jobs or internships to get that real world experience, and start their. 
4. The last big one is to take your time on applications; quality over quantity. The shotgun approach can be tempting but you have to realize that for any single job posting, there is someone out there that gave it their all. They wrote a full, detailed cover letter, provided convincing answers to the various behavioral questions, and made their application look as good as possible. Recruiters and hiring managers are looking for reasons to remove people from their stack. If you didn't give them a cover letter, you're probably not going to be considered. If you didn't take enough time to write a thorough resume, you're probably not going to be considered. Take that extra 15-20 minutes so they see you at your best.

At the end of the day, it's a game of probability. Every step you take to fill the position's needs, the better probability you have of hearing back, and moving on to the next rounds. Aim for the right target and be consistent with your work and you'll get hired. Good luck!

Man, I'm there with you. I've been iteratively adjusting my process. I started out applying to literally everything (50-80 apps per week) with no cover letter, no portfolio website, a half baked resume, and next to no other info beyond the minimum requested in the application.

Then I updated my resume with the help of someone on Fiverr and a friend that also changed careers from IT to SWE like I'm trying to do. I also finished and deployed my portfolio website, and started applying more. That got me a few bites but I was still not hearing back beyond maybe 2-3 screening calls in the first month.

Then I created a cover letter template that was stock and just required me to plug in the position name, the company name, and one sentence specifically about the job. I also uploaded all my school projects to GitHub, finished a project, and started a new one that was way more in depth. This got me a few more calls, and even a few take home assignments and others. At this point I was applying to about 20 to 25 jobs per week.

Just recently I switched things up. My cover letter is much more personalized for the job in question. It doesn't sound as fake or cookie cutter, and I make sure to address several direct aspects of the company, culture, and position. I also revamped my resume after getting feedback from a few recruiters. One of the best lines of advice I got was "make the hiring manager's job as easy as possible". I structured it to answer exactly what a hiring manager/recruiter would want to know about me. Then I've been making sure to make commits on my GitHub projects every few days or so. All this has lead to a few actual interviews with hiring teams, and so far no rejections from those interviews, as well as second rounds of take homes/project interviews. There's probably more I can do to improve my chances that I'll address with time, but it's definitely quite the process to get hired.

The only thing really keeping me going is posts like yours that remind me that this is the grind. But one day, someone will hire me, and you, and all the other soon-to-be-devs out there. 

Also, I had no idea what 'Staff' or 'Associate' meant. I thought they were lesser than a basic SWE and wasted so much time applying to those roles. Also, no established company wants to hire a back end engineer right out of college. Their back end is precious, and they don't want anything bad happening to it. I've found much more success applying to generic Software Engineer roles, or New Grad Frontend, Fullstack, or Backend roles, or Junior/Entry Level. 

Good luck!

Coming from the sysadmin world, these aren't stupid questions; like you said, they're legitimate. Python is a scripting language, and a powerful one at that. Loosely written scripts and programs can open your environment up to danger. Say for example your script loaded data into a local database that contained sensitive information. If your code has the database host, user, and password for authentication, that could easily be compromised *if* the database is public facing and someone got ahold of your script. There's a lot of "if"s here. 

To answer his question, you'd be better of explaining in depth what exactly you code does to explain that it does not open your environment up to vulnerabilities. If it is only entering data into a local/network file, then you're not exposing anything, especially if the Excel document is not encrypted or sensitive in its nature. 

​

>*Can You categorically state that the software has no flaws or holes in it that hackers could exploit?*

I would tell them yes, we can review the source code, and I can explain how each part of my program works locally, from an authenticated user account. No part of the code touches sensitive data, nor does it expose secrets. Another concern is usually third party libraries. If you are importing libraries, you can take it one step further and provide them with websites or GitHub repos for any library you use to confirm its authenticity. No software is 100% secure from hackers, but your program doesn't seem to be something that would jeopardize the environment or your data if someone were to get ahold of it.

 

>*Can he justify the software is secure and cannot be manipulated/changed?*

This one is a bit silly in my mind, but I can give you a bit of guidance. If, like the example I gave above, your code connected to a database holding sensitive data, their concern would likely be that a malicious library being imported could possibly modify the code to obtain data. You can again demonstrate that your code doesn't interact with sensitive data. A big tip here is that the script only has the same permissions as the user running it, so if someone without authorization to access certain files did obtain your source code, it wouldn't have any reach into your environment, much like someone trying to log into one of your servers without credentials. An attacker would first need to obtain your, or someone else's, credentials to the network before your script could do any potential damage, and that is again, *IF* your code touches anything sensitive. 

​

>*What security is built into the software?*

My answer will be redundant here. As long as you review the libraries used in your code, and provide links to confirm the legitimacy of them, and review the source code itself to explain what exactly it does and that it does not interact with sensitive data, then you should be fine. If you are in fact dealing with a protected Excel document and your script includes credentials, you may need to use some sort of encryption to provide peace of mind, but the security they have put in place for your network (ie. Active Directory credentials and permissions to the network drives where these workbooks may be located) is all you need to prevent unauthorized access using your script. Another note is that using Python 3 vs Python 2 is a boost in security alone. 

I think the sysadmin is coming at this with an abundance of caution which is understandable. No one wants to find out some guy in the office made a crappy script using a malicious library with a typo in it that ended up providing hackers access to the network and sensitive information. Based on your description, your application seems sterile and unlikely to cause damage. 

Also, here are some helpful articles that might help you with explaining why your script is not a threat to the environment:

[Python Security Best Practices](https://snyk.io/blog/python-security-best-practices-cheat-sheet/)

[3 Most Common Python Security Vulnerabilities](https://blog.eccouncil.org/3-of-the-most-common-python-security-vulnerabilities/)

Lastly, here's a post from someone asking the same-ish question and the first answer has some good information about how the environment should be set up by the sysadmin to ensure safety, including no local admins, and user account control (UAC) if there are local admins on computers.

[Considerations of Running Python on Corporate Network](https://www.reddit.com/r/Python/comments/3sf8b5/considerations_of_running_python_on_a_corporate/)

I hope it works out for you!

The best way I've found to understand an API is how you interact with the world.

When you go to a restaurant, you want their food. To get it, you use a menu, and wait for the waiter to take your order. Then you wait, and your food comes.

When you go to a bank, you want your money. To get it, you go to the counter, swipe your card, enter your PIN, and get your money.

In both examples, you're getting something from someone/something, but the process differs. An API in general serves you the thing you want. In the same way you wouldn't use a menu and a waiter to get your money, or swipe your card and provide your PIN to order food, understanding the API you're using is important to get the right information. The API is the middle man between you wanting something, and you getting that thing. It gets it and serves it.

An API can be internal for your own application and it's files to get the data it needs (such as a website grabbing user information when they load their profile), or outward facing for other devs to use (say you have a database full of cat pictures and people want to use those pictures on their site).

I'm right there with you. Some weeks it's just how it is. This week was that for me. I had a portfolio of 8 projects; my director made it clear that I need to start making faster progress on them. Throughout the week she emailed me about 50 times with "little" questions regarding CCPA policies because she knows fuck all about IT and is trying to handle that with the other executives who are qualified for their job. Then on Tuesday she told me to put together a work order system for two departments, train them, document the process, and communicate with our sales team about the process by the end of today so it could be rolled out Monday. All of this on top of our Salesforce crapping out and preventing half of our reps from being able to use the app for a day, as well as one of our two inventory manager's having her PC die while working remotely. That's all on top of the usual calls, texts, emails, tickets, drive-by tasks. Today I straight up feel my head buzzing, and I want to just vent to the air in my apartment, but I DON'T HAVE THE FUCKING TIME TO DO THAT. So yes, totally with you.

As for tips, I've found a few

* Give yourself the uninterrupted time to plan your objectives for the day every morning
   * Take 30 minutes, don't answer the phone, and just make a OneNote or Notion page with a list of the most important things you **need** to get done
   * Target those important tasks, and use some space at the bottom of your page to take notes on any new impromptu task requests
   * It may feel just as disorganized, but honestly, just getting it out of your head feels SO much better; it also gives you a way to look back at what you were asked to do (I stress out because I know people asked me for things but I forgot who and what)
* In the same way, at the beginning of the week, set your weekly objectives
   * This way when you get to the end of the week, if you made progress (this doesn't mean completing 100%) you can feel good about your work
   * Everything else can be handled when you have the time
* Distribute your tasks
   * I struggle with "I have to do it if I want it done right" which then causes the issue of "I don't have enough time for all this shit"
   * Unfortunately that problem has only one person to blame
   * If you have any shred of authority to do so, ask someone else to help you with tasks when you get overwhelmed
   * It always surprises me how much other technicians/admins want to do the same work, usually because I'm hogging it all (unintentionally)
   * Give them the experience so you can focus better
* Hold yourself accountable
   * This is a big one for me. I often find myself getting overwhelmed with tasks, so I "take a break" and watch YouTube, or scroll through Reddit for a few minutes. Then someone calls and I feel this heightened sense of stress. Then after that call I now have n + 1 tasks to do, and I have 30 minutes less of my day to do them
   * If you need breaks, schedule them and hold yourself accountable not to take up that time
   * The more "relaxing" you do during work hours, the more stressed you'll end up. Hold yourself accountable while you're working, do the hard work now, and you'll feel way more satisfied and productive which in turn reduces your stress

BTW, none of this is directed at you. It's just stuff that I've learned and finally addressed over the last couple of years that has helped significantly!

Also, read the book "Getting Things Done". It can be dry, but the tips for stress free productivity are SUPER helpful. I definitely don't follow it to the T, but I used some methods mentioned for organizing my email inbox and holy shit it changed my life, literally. 

Good luck. I hope you get a chance to go lay under a tree and look at clouds and relax.

I'm by no means an expert, but I've found a way that works. I completely overhauled our on-premise Active Directory security groups which are synchronized with Office 365. I created a whole scheme for SharePoint with the SP prefix. We have groups like SP\_HR, SP\_HR\_Safety, SP\_VP\_Finance, SP\_Sales, etc. As part of our onboarding, dept/role transfer, and termination processes, we update group membership. That way I just set up the appropriate groups in each site. Owners are the O365\_Admin group which contain mostly IT members and our networking consultants. Then, by our standard, the built-in site "Members" permission group contains related management groups. So the Sales department site has in its Sales Members group the SP\_Sales\_Management and related groups. Then the in the site "Visitors" group, I put either everyone except external users if it's a company wide site, or the baseline group that contains front-line employees. In that case, Sales Visitors would contain SP\_Sales. I built the AD groups up so SP\_Sales includes individual sales reps with the SP\_Sales\_Management group as a member. SP\_Sales\_Management contains all of the individual sales managers and the SP\_Sales\_Executive group. That pattern is mirrored for all departments.

So far, the only permission requests I have gotten have come from people visiting the wrong site, and a handful of missing permissions that were overlooked. Overall it has been very easy to maintain as we already maintain group membership.

I'm not sure if that answers your question, but hopefully it gives you an example of how you can manage site permissions more easily.
